name: IDRA-21

card.summary: A research AMPA-receptor modulator studied in animals for memory and learning, which is why it appears in nootropic circles aiming for sharper focus and recall.
card.note: Research chemical with no human trials; animal work reports increased neuron injury after ischemia.

quick.overview:
IDRA-21 is a benzothiadiazine compound that positively modulates AMPA-type glutamate receptors. Fidia Farmaceutici in Italy investigated it in the 1990s as a possible treatment for memory problems, and it has remained a research tool.

In animal studies it improved performance on memory and learning tasks in monkeys, at oral doses reported to be far lower than those of the related compound aniracetam. Community interest comes from this cognitive-enhancement research.
quick.mechanism: It slows the desensitization and deactivation of AMPA receptors, so excitatory glutamate signals last longer and are stronger. Lab work also found it reduces NMDA-receptor currents in cultured neurons, and that it influences long-term potentiation, a cellular correlate of learning.
quick.risks: No human clinical data have been reported. In rats, doses given orally increased hippocampal neuron loss after induced ischemia, and the authors noted that AMPA potentiation could matter in conditions such as stroke or seizures. It is not an approved medicine.

chain: Improved memory task performance in animals
angle.text: Users interested in IDRA-21 are after sharper memory, learning and focus, which feed into study, work and presence. The supporting research is in animals and cells; it has not been tested in people.

lead: IDRA-21 (7-chloro-3-methyl-3,4-dihydro-2H-1,2,4-benzothiadiazine S,S-dioxide) is a synthetic positive allosteric modulator of AMPA glutamate receptors, studied as a cognitive enhancer [1][2]. People interested in it hope for better memory and mental sharpness, which supports performance in work and study.

It reduces AMPA receptor desensitization, prolonging excitatory synaptic currents [3][4]. In monkeys it improved delayed-matching and visual recognition memory tasks [5][6] and reversed learning impairment induced by alprazolam [7].
It was developed by Fidia Farmaceutici in the 1990s; development was reported discontinued in 2003, and no human clinical data have been reported [1].

paras: No studies found. In animal and cell research, IDRA-21 improved delayed-matching performance in young and aged rhesus monkeys [5], enhanced visual recognition memory in young macaques [6], and abated alprazolam-induced cognitive impairment in patas monkeys [7]. In hippocampal slices it affected long-term potentiation [8].

IDRA-21 attenuates rapid AMPA receptor desensitization and slows deactivation, facilitating excitatory transmission [2][1]. In rat cerebellar granule neurons it showed lower intrinsic activity than cyclothiazide and was not neurotoxic in that preparation up to 100 micromolar [3]. It also inhibited NMDA receptor currents in cultured cells, with more effect on NR2B-containing receptors [4]. Structural work has examined the thiazide binding site on the GluR2 receptor [9].

Reviews note that excessive AMPA activation can cause excitotoxicity, as in seizures or ischemia [2]. In one study, oral IDRA-21 increased CA1 hippocampal neuron loss after global ischemia in rats, and killed cultured neurons in the presence of glutamate [10]. No human safety data are available.

Fidia Farmaceutici investigated IDRA-21 in the 1990s for memory impairments linked to aging, drug-induced deficits and ischemia; the program was reported discontinued in 2003 [1]. Key early papers appeared in 1995-1997 [7][3].
